title: Formal framing: social cognition within the EFE / compression / empowerment stack

html:
Within the formal architecture developed above, social cognition does not require new first principles–it is the application of the same EFE-minimizing, compression-seeking, empowerment-maximizing machinery to a domain whose generative structure happens to be recursive and reflexive. Consider the problem facing an agent ii that must select policies in an environment containing agent jj. To minimize expected free energy, agent ii needs a generative model Pi(oτi,sτi,sτj∣πi)P_i(o^i_\tau, s^i_\tau, s^j_\tau \mid \pi^i) that includes the hidden states of agent jj–crucially, jj’s beliefs, goals, and policy. But jj’s policy is itself a function of jj’s model of ii: πj=f(Pj(sτi))\pi^j = f(P_j(s^i_\tau)). This yields the characteristic recursive embedding of social cognition: ii must model jj modeling ii (and, in principle, jj modeling ii modeling jj, ad infinitum). In practice, this recursion is truncated–human adults appear to reliably handle approximately two to three levels of recursive mentalizing ("I believe that you believe that I intend...") before performance degrades 1, 2–but even truncated recursive inference over hidden mental states is a compression problem of extraordinary depth. Each "other-model" is itself a generative model (with latent variables for beliefs, desires, temperament, knowledge states, and social commitments) that must be learned, maintained, and updated from sparse, noisy behavioral observations–and the number of such models scales with social group size, imposing the representational demands that have been argued to drive primate neocortical expansion 3, 4.

Compression progress in the social domain takes a distinctive form: because other agents are partially observable systems generating behavior from hidden generative models, "compressing" social experience means discovering the latent trait and state variables (personality dimensions, attachment styles, social roles, cultural identities, moral commitments) that render others’ behavior predictable across contexts. A good social model is one that achieves low description length over the behavioral stream of a social partner–explaining their choices, utterances, and emotional displays as the output of a compact set of stable dispositions modulated by contextual states. This is why humans spontaneously construct character models of familiar others (trait attributions, narrative identities, relational schemas) and why violations of expected character ("that’s so unlike her") generate large social prediction errors that demand model revision. The same compression logic applies reflexively to the self-model: the agent’s representation of its own dispositions, values, and social commitments functions as a generative prior over its own future behavior, and maintaining a coherent self-model is equivalent to maintaining a low-complexity, high-predictive-accuracy model of oneself–an identity.

Empowerment in the social domain–social empowerment–is the capacity to reliably influence the behavior and internal states of other agents. Formally, it is the channel capacity of the agent’s social action repertoire (utterances, gestures, facial expressions, favors, threats, reputation signals) with respect to others’ future states (beliefs, emotions, cooperation decisions, resource allocations). Social empowerment is uniquely challenging because the "channel" is non-stationary (the other agent adapts) and partially adversarial (the other agent may resist influence or attempt counter-influence)–making other agents simultaneously the highest-value and highest-difficulty targets for empowerment maximization. Critically, social empowerment is bidirectional: the agent’s capacity to influence others depends on others’ willingness to be influenced, which in turn depends on the agent’s reputation, trustworthiness, group membership, and perceived alignment with shared norms. This creates a fundamental interdependence: maximizing long-run social empowerment requires the agent to constrain its own short-run behavior (honoring commitments, adhering to norms, investing in relationships) in ways that build and maintain the social capital upon which future influence depends. In other words, social norms and relational bonds are not merely external constraints on the agent’s optimization but are instrumentally optimal strategies for sustained social empowerment–and, through internalization, they become part of the agent’s own preference landscape (entering the P(oτ)P(o_\tau) term of EFE as learned priors over social outcomes).

The risk term of EFE is also profoundly reshaped by social embedding. For a hypersocial, obligately cooperative species like Homo sapiens, social exclusion is not merely unpleasant but constitutes a viability threat comparable in severity to starvation or predation: across ancestral environments, loss of group membership meant loss of access to shared food, cooperative defense, mating opportunities, and cultural knowledge, making exclusion tantamount to a death sentence 5, 6. Evolution has accordingly installed social exclusion as a deep viability prior–social rejection activates neural circuitry (dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, anterior insula) that overlaps substantially with circuits processing physical pain 7, 8, and the threat of exclusion is sufficient to override other motivational signals (hunger, fatigue, personal gain) in favor of socially conforming behavior 9. This means that a substantial portion of the human preference distribution P(oτ)P(o_\tau) is allocated to social outcomes: being included, being valued, being seen as trustworthy and competent, occupying a recognized role in a social group. The "risk" that human EFE minimization works to avoid is not only physiological (hypoglycemia, hypothermia) but deeply and irreducibly social (rejection, humiliation, reputational collapse, norm violation and its punitive consequences). Identity, attachment, and norm compliance are therefore not luxuries pursued after survival needs are met; they are themselves survival-relevant variables that occupy privileged positions in the organism’s viability manifold.
